subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Persepolis: Burned by Alexander
description: A fast breakdown of Persepolis: Burned by Alexander for builders.

hook.text: The capital of the Persian Empire was the richest city on Earth. Alexander the Great burned it down in one night.

buildup.text: Darius I built Persepolis around 515 BCE. Twenty-three nations sent tribute and are carved into its staircases.

discovery.text: The Apadana staircase shows delegates in perfect detail — hairstyles, clothing, and gifts from across the empire.

twist.text: Alexander may have burned it in a drunken rage or as revenge for Persia's destruction of Athens. Historians disagree.

climax.text: The fire preserved thousands of clay tablets by baking them hard. Destruction accidentally saved the archives.

punchline.text: The fire that destroyed an empire accidentally preserved its records forever.

quiz.question: How did the fire at Persepolis accidentally help archaeology?
options: It melted gold into a solid mass that preserved inscriptions
It baked thousands of clay tablets hard, preserving the archives
It created an ash layer that sealed artifacts from decay

details.summary: Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, was built by Darius I around 515 BCE as a showcase of imperial power. Its massive stone terraces, audience halls, and carved reliefs depicted tribute from 23 nations. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BCE.
details.whyItMatters: Persepolis represents the peak of Achaemenid art and architecture. Its carved reliefs depicting diverse peoples bringing tribute document the multicultural Persian Empire, which governed the largest territory the ancient world had yet seen.
takeaways: Ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire, built around 515 BCE
Relief carvings depict representatives of 23 subject nations
Burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE

faq.question: Why did Alexander burn Persepolis?
faq.answer: Ancient sources disagree. Some say it was deliberate revenge for the Persian burning of Athens in 480 BCE. Others claim it was an impulsive act during a drunken banquet. The destruction may have served a political message — signaling the end of the Persian Empire and the beginning of Alexander's.

faq.question: What survived the burning?
faq.answer: Stone columns, terraces, staircases, and carved relief sculptures survived because they could not burn. The Apadana reliefs — showing representatives of subject peoples bearing tribute — are among the finest works of ancient Near Eastern art. The site remains Iran's most important cultural monument.
